fields.title: What breaks the client
fields.keyTakeaway: Adding to a contract is safe; removing and redefining are not, and the safety of addition is ensured by how clients are written, not just the server.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Which API changes are safe, and which will stop user applications and partner integrations?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: A [[breaking-change|breaking change]] released without preparation leads to app failures for some users and halts partner integrations. Recovery takes hours, reputational damage—longer. A product manager who knows the boundary distinguishes a fix from a project during planning, rather than during rollback.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: An [[additive-change|additive change]] is safe. A breaking one is not. The boundary runs as follows:
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/items/0: Add a new field to the response
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/items/3: Expand the range of values where the client does not enumerate them
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/items/4: Relax validation: make a required field optional
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/items/1: Change field type: string became a number
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/items/3: Change the meaning of a field while keeping the same name—the most insidious, because nothing crashes
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/items/4: Add a new value to an enumeration if the client crashes on unknown values
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/items/5: Change identifier format, error code, nesting structure
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: The last item on the safe list deserves special attention. Adding a new status value—`in_transit`, alongside existing `accepted` and `delivered`—is safe only if clients are written as [[tolerant-reader|tolerant readers]]: they ignore unfamiliar values instead of crashing. This is a property of the client, not the server, and it is ensured by convention, not technology.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: Hence the practical rule: **contracts must be designed for growth.** A list of values is accompanied by a note that new ones may appear. Clients are written so that unfamiliar fields are ignored.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: The case with the order `status` field. We added the value `assembling` between `accepted` and `in_transit`—it seemed like an additive change.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: The mobile app displayed statuses via a hardcoded list and showed an empty tracking screen for unknown values. We spotted the problem a day later through support tickets. Rollback wasn't possible—orders in that status already existed. We rushed an emergency release and waited three weeks for users to update.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: After that, the mobile app contract was updated with a rule: the server always returns `status` and `status_display_text`. The client displays the text, but builds its logic on the status, falling back to neutral behavior on unfamiliar values. New statuses have been added three times since then without a single incident.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: For the partner API, the rule was documented in a separate section: the value list is open, handle unfamiliar values as "other".
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: The tolerant reader solves the problem of additions, but not removals or meaning changes. For those, versions are needed—the next lesson.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Adding to a contract is safe; removing and redefining are not, and the safety of addition is ensured by how clients are written, not just the server.
